I don't think Aristotle requires a steady-state eternal universe, just that it could still be allowed without affecting the prime mover argument.

That is, if you tell someone there is a first mover, they might object that the universe has an infinite backward timeline, thinking that removes the need for the first mover.

But Aristotle assumes the infinite universe in order to show that the prime mover argument goes through all the same. Assuming the infinite backward timeline is a way of addressing this common objection before it is raised.

I don't think anything in Aristotle's philosophy hinges on an infinite backward timeline.

The assumption isn't like, "We think this is the case, so let's see what follows."

The assumption is more like, "Even if this is the case, the conclusion of the prime mover still follows."

So, it's not like Aristotle could be proven wrong about this. It was not essential to his position. Nothing hinges on it.

There are various views in philosophy of time; namely, presentism and eternalism. There isn't yet a clear winner such that the unreality of time can be declared.
